interactions: Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: CYP2C9 inhibition raises phenytoin levels; toxicity risk; monitor free levels or choose another agent.
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + atorvastatin: CYP3A4 induction lowers atorvastatin exposure.
Levetiracetam: no clinically relevant interaction with the current medications; renally cleared, dose by creatinine clearance.
Valproate: no major interaction with the current medications; monitor ammonia and platelets.
Lacosamide: dose-related PR prolongation; obtain an ECG before IV loading.
Acyclovir + trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: additive nephrotoxicity risk; trimethoprim also blocks tubular creatinine secretion, so creatinine may rise without a fall in GFR.
Trimethoprim + lisinopril: additive hyperkalemia; monitor potassium.
Metformin: hold if renal function falls during IV acyclovir.
output.proposed: Lorazepam, a second-line antiseizure medication (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate or lacosamide) and IV acyclovir with metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and cetirizine
warnings: IV acyclovir: crystal nephropathy; give IV fluids and dose by renal function.

output.query: HSV encephalitis with status epilepticus: antiviral treatment and second-line antiseizure medication

results.finding: Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 14 to 21 days is the treatment of choice for HSV encephalitis, started on suspicion.
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus.
Continuous EEG monitoring is advised for at least 24 hours in comatose or non-convulsive status epilepticus.

output.summary: HSV encephalitis is treated with IV acyclovir for 14 to 21 days [Tunkel_2008]. The three second-line agents for status epilepticus are equally effective [ESETT_2019]. Non-convulsive status is monitored with continuous EEG [Brophy_2012].

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric acyclovir while waiting for HSV PCR: early treatment improves outcome.
Do NOT perform the lumbar puncture before CT excludes mass effect in this patient with focal signs and GCS 11.
Do NOT stop acyclovir early once HSV-1 PCR is positive: treat for 14 to 21 days.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours, adjusted for renal function, immediately and without waiting for imaging or CSF, and continue it for 14 to 21 days for confirmed HSV encephalitis [Tunkel_2008].

Give IV fluids during acyclovir and monitor creatinine to prevent crystal nephropathy, and stop trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole if the UTI course is complete or switch to a non-nephrotoxic agent [Tunkel_2008].
Load a second-line ASM: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid fosphenytoin because trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole inhibits phenytoin metabolism [ESETT_2019].
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

key_clinical_evidence: HSV encephalitis typically involves one temporal lobe, the insula and the cingulate gyrus, with mesial temporal FLAIR and DWI signal
Empiric acyclovir starts as soon as HSV encephalitis is suspected [Tunkel_2008]
Post-HSV NMDAR encephalitis can emerge during recovery; repeat neuronal antibody testing if he deteriorates after antiviral treatment
Non-convulsive status epilepticus accompanies HSV encephalitis in many patients and needs both antiviral and antiseizure treatment
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole raises phenytoin levels, which favors levetiracetam as the second-line agent

patient.history_present_illness: A 66-year-old Hispanic male retired mechanic was brought to the emergency department by his son, who witnessed a brief tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. The patient has no known history of epilepsy. His son reports that over the past 2 weeks, his father had been having progressive memory difficulty, confusion, and behavioral changes: he kept repeating questions, got lost driving to a familiar gas station, and had been sleeping 14-16 hours per day. He had also complained of intermittent headaches. No fever at home was noted initially. After the brief shaking stopped, the patient did not return to baseline. Instead, over the following 20 minutes, the son noticed his father making repetitive unusual hand and finger movements, rubbing his thumb and index finger together continuously, and intermittently smacking his lips. EMS temperature was 38.2°C. He has a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia but no neurological conditions. He takes metformin, lisinopril and atorvastatin. Recently, his primary care physician started him on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for a urinary tract infection 12 days ago. He also takes over-the-counter cetirizine for seasonal allergies. No known immunosuppression. Son denies alcohol use, illicit drugs, or recent travel outside the state. No sick contacts. No known tuberculosis exposure. Family history: father had Alzheimer's dementia at 78. Wife died of breast cancer. Son and daughter healthy.
